content: Loratadine is an antihistamine approved by the FDA for the treatment of symptoms such as a runny nose, sneezing, itchy and watery eyes, and itching of the nose or throat. Common side effects include dry mouth, headache, drowsiness, and fatigue. For adults, the FDA-approved dosage for seasonal allergic rhinitis and idiopathic urticaria is 10 mg taken orally once daily. Off-label uses in adults include asthma (10-20 mg orally daily for up to 8 weeks) and eosinophilic nonallergic rhinitis, though limited information is available for these indications. In pediatric patients, the FDA-approved dosage for seasonal allergic rhinitis and idiopathic urticaria is 5 mg orally daily for children aged 2-5 years and 10 mg orally daily for children aged 6 years and older. Off-label use in pediatric asthma includes 10 mg orally daily for children weighing less than 30 kg and 20 mg orally daily for those weighing more than 30 kg. Limited information is available regarding off-label guideline-supported use in pediatric patients. Loratadine is contraindicated in individuals with hypersensitivity to the drug. Patients with liver or kidney disease should consult a doctor before use, as dose adjustments may be necessary. Overuse of loratadine can cause drowsiness, and any allergic reaction to the medication should prompt immediate discontinuation and medical consultation. Pregnant or breastfeeding individuals should seek advice from a healthcare professional before use. The medication should be kept out of reach of children, and in case of overdose, medical help or contact with a Poison Control Center is advised. Adverse reactions reported during clinical trials include rash (dermatologic), abdominal pain, diarrhea, stomatitis, and dry mouth (gastrointestinal), as well as hepatic necrosis, hepatitis, and jaundice (hepatic). Neurologic side effects include anxiety, headache, hyperactivity, and drowsiness. Respiratory effects include nosebleeds, pharyngitis, upper respiratory infections, viral disease, and wheezing. Other reported effects include dysphonia, fatigue, flu-like symptoms, malaise, somnolence, and tooth disorders. Postmarketing data on loratadine is limited. Drug interactions include QT interval prolongation and Torsade de Pointes when co-administered with amiodarone. Loratadine increases plasma concentrations of carbamazepine, cimetidine, and ketoconazole. It also increases the risk of paralytic ileus when used with morphine, morphine sulfate liposome, or oxymorphone. Interactions with mepenzolate and umeclidinium are also noted. Loratadine is classified as Pregnancy Category B by the FDA and Category B1 in Australia. There is no specific guidance on its use during labor and delivery, in nursing mothers, or in geriatric, gender-specific, racial, renal-impaired, hepatic-impaired, or immunocompromised populations. The drug is administered orally and is well absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract. It undergoes rapid first-pass hepatic metabolism, primarily via cytochrome P450 enzymes (CYP3A4, CYP2D6, and others). Loratadine is highly bound to plasma proteins (97-99%), and its active metabolite, desloratadine, is 73-76% protein-bound. Limited information is available on its nonclinical toxicology and clinical studies. Loratadine is supplied as 10 mg tablets in 30and 40-tablet cartons. It should be stored at 20°-25°C (68°-77°F). Alcohol interaction with loratadine has not been established, and patients should consult their doctor regarding alcohol use while on this medication. Brand names for loratadine include Alavert, Claritin, Claritin Reditabs, Clearatadine, Triaminic Allerchews, Children's Clear-Atadine, Children's Dimetapp ND Allergy, and Children's Claritin. There is limited information on look-alike drug names for loratadine.
